power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: Color preferences in dogs: Replication of Roy et al. 2025 (May 2025)
table.existing_data_explanation: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions: Replicating Roy et al. (2025), we ask whether dogs are more likely to choose a yellow bowl over a blue or grey bowl when presented with the three colors.
table.design_dependent_variables: Number of first choices for each bowl color. Experimenters will observe the choice and record the order of bowl colors chosen. Each dog will experience one choice.
table.study_design_overview: All dogs will experience a single condition involving a single choice between yellow, blue, and grey bowls with treats in them.
table.statistical_tests: We will conduct a Chi-square test comparing the frequency of first choices across the three bowl colors against a null (chance) expectation. We will also calculate Cramér's V as a measure of effect size. To replicate Roy et al., we will draw inferences based on the frequentist Chi-square test. But we will also calculate Bayes factors for this using Bayesian multinomial tests in JASP.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Based on Roy et al. (2025), we will exclude subjects when the bowls are not equidistant or the proper distance from the subject, the experimenter is not positioned correctly, or other dogs or humans interfere with the testing session.

7) How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size? No need to justify decision, but be precise about exactly how the number will be determined.
We will collect data until we have complete sessions from 75 dogs to match the sample in the food condition of Roy et al. (2025).

8) Anything else you would like to pre-register? (e.g., secondary analyses, variables collected for exploratory purposes, unusual analyses planned?)
We collected data from 3 pilot subjects on 2025-04-29 to test out the procedure. We will not be using those three data points in our analysis.

table.title: Color preferences in young dogs: June 2025
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Replicating Roy et al. (2025), we hypothesize that dogs are more likely to choose a yellow bowl over a blue or grey bowl when presented with the three colors. We also hypothesize that the presence of food, dog sex, and bowl position will not affect the color preference.
table.design_dependent_variables: Number of first choices for each bowl color. Experimenters will observe the choice and record the order of bowl colors chosen. Each dog will experience one choice.
table.study_design_overview: There will be two between-subjects conditions: with and without food. In the with food condition, a treat will be in each of the three bowls. In the no food condition, no treats will be in any bowls. All dogs will choose between yellow, blue, and grey bowls (in counterbalanced position across dogs).
table.statistical_tests: We will conduct a Chi-square test comparing the frequency of first choices across the three bowl colors for the with and no food conditions against a null (chance) expectation. If there is no effect of the presence of food, we will combine these into a single analysis of color. We will also conduct Chi-square tests of the effect of dog sex and bowl position (left, center, right). We will also calculate Cramér's V as a measure of effect size for all analyses. To replicate Roy et al., we will draw inferences based on the frequentist Chi-square test. But we will also calculate Bayes factors for this using Bayesian multinomial tests in JASP/R.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Based on Roy et al. (2025), we will exclude subjects when the bowls are not equidistant or the proper distance from the subject, the experimenter is not positioned correctly, or other dogs or humans interfere with the testing session. In addition, we will exclude/not test dogs older than six years old.

7) How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size? No need to justify decision, but be precise about exactly how the number will be determined.
We will collect data until we have complete sessions from 76 dogs in the with food condition and 58 in the no food condition to match the samples of Roy et al. (2025).

8) Anything else you would like to pre-register? (e.g., secondary analyses, variables collected for exploratory purposes, unusual analyses planned?)
This is a follow-up to our previously pre-registered study of 75 dogs in the with food condition (but with no age restriction).

table.title: Brightness preference in young dogs: September 2025
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: We will present dogs with three grey bowls of varying brightness: light, medium, and dark grey. We hypothesize that dogs are more likely to choose the brightest bowl over either of the two darker bowls. We also hypothesize that the dog sex and bowl position will not affect the brightness preference.
table.design_dependent_variables: Number of first choices for each bowl brightness level (light, medium, dark). Experimenters will observe the choice and record the order of bowl brightness levels chosen. Each dog will experience one choice.
table.study_design_overview: All dogs will choose between light, medium, and dark grey bowls (in counterbalanced position across dogs).
table.statistical_tests: We will conduct a Chi-square test comparing the frequency of first choices across the three bowl brightness levels against a null (chance) expectation. We will also conduct Chi-square tests of the effect of dog sex and bowl position (left, center, right). We will also calculate Cramér's V as a measure of effect size for all analyses. To replicate Roy et al., we will draw inferences based on the frequentist Chi-square test. But we will also calculate Bayes factors for this using Bayesian multinomial tests in JASP/R.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Based on Roy et al. (2025), we will exclude subjects when the bowls are not equidistant or the proper distance from the subject, the experimenter is not positioned correctly, or other dogs or humans interfere with the testing session. In addition, we will exclude/not test dogs older than six years old.

7) How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size? No need to justify decision, but be precise about exactly how the number will be determined.
We will collect data until we have complete sessions from 150 dogs or until Oct 31st, 2025. The sample size of 150 matches the sample size of the full data set from our previous color experiment that showed a preference for yellow bowls.

8) Anything else you would like to pre-register? (e.g., secondary analyses, variables collected for exploratory purposes, unusual analyses planned?)
Nothing else to pre-register.

A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Free-ranging dogs (Canis familiaris) in India have been shown to prefer approaching yellow bowls before blue and grey ones (Roy et al. (2025).
text.formatted: Free-ranging dogs (Canis familiaris) in India have been shown to prefer approaching yellow bowls before blue and grey ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Roy et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: Animal Cognition, 28(1), 1-9).
However, it is not clear if this preference for the color yellow is specific to free-ranging dogs in India or whether it generalizes to other dog populations.
We conducted a replication of the Roy et al. study to assess whether pet dogs in the United States show similar preferences by measuring whether they approached yellow, blue, or grey bowls first.
We conducted two experiments and found that pet dogs younger than seven years old first approached yellow bowls most often, replicating Roy et al.'s findings.
To test if brightness rather than color accounted for this preference, we conducted a third preference experiment with light, medium, and dark grey bowls.
The dogs did not prefer the light grey bowl, indicating that there was not a preference for the brightest achromatic stimulus.
Therefore, a preference for yellow food-related objects extends beyond free-ranging dogs to our sample of pet dogs.

Understanding dog color preferences is important for guiding the design of dog products and environments but also is critical for canine behavioral scientists who must make decisions about colors for experimental stimuli.
Color can provide information about the fitness of potential mates, the ripeness of fruits, or the toxicity of prey (Cuthill et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Color can provide information about the fitness of potential mates, the ripeness of fruits, or the toxicity of prey <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cuthill et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, animals may have preferences for some colors over others.
However, different species have different color perception abilities.

For instance, dogs (Canis familiaris) lack a medium-wave color photoreceptor that humans have, giving them a different visual color palette (Rosengren, 1969; Neitz et al., 1989; Jacobs et al., 1993; Tanaka et al., 2000; Kasparson et al., 2013; Pongrácz et al., 2017; Byosiere et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For instance, dogs (Canis familiaris) lack a medium-wave color photoreceptor that humans have, giving them a different visual color palette <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rosengren, 1969;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Neitz et al., 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Jacobs et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Tanaka et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kasparson et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Pongrácz et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Byosiere et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work by Roy et al. (2025) suggests that Indian free-ranging dogs use color information to make decisions about potential sources of food.
text.formatted: Recent work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> suggests that Indian free-ranging dogs use color information to make decisions about potential sources of food.

text.text: When offered food in three different colored bowls, Indian free-ranging dogs preferred a yellow bowl over a blue or grey bowl.
However, it is not clear whether the experience of living as a free-ranging dog in India drives this preference or whether it is a property of dogs more generally.
The present study replicates and expands on Roy et al. to determine whether pet dogs in the United States also demonstrate a preference for yellow.
text.formatted: The present study replicates and expands on <ref type="bibr">Roy et al.</ref> to determine whether pet dogs in the United States also demonstrate a preference for yellow.

text.text: We replicate the methods of Roy et al. in a different population in two experiments and expand on their work by testing a potential alternative account for our findings in a third experiment.
text.formatted: We replicate the methods of <ref type="bibr">Roy et al.</ref> in a different population in two experiments and expand on their work by testing a potential alternative account for our findings in a third experiment.

text.text: Pet dogs live with humans and experience much of the colorful world that we surround ourselves with.
From toys and furniture to bowls and leashes, we directly interact with dogs using colorful objects.
However, looking at the same stimuli does not mean seeing the same colors given dogs' more limited color vision capabilities.
Visual discrimination tasks allow dogs to show us what they can distinguish in their environment by training dogs to select a specific colored stimulus.

Using these (and similar) methods, discrimination studies demonstrate that dogs can distinguish between colors (Rosengren, 1969; Neitz et al., 1989; Tanaka et al., 2000), showing a clear ability to distinguish blue and yellow (Kasparson et al., 2013; Pongrácz et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Using these (and similar) methods, discrimination studies demonstrate that dogs can distinguish between colors <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rosengren, 1969;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Neitz et al., 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Tanaka et al., 2000)</ref>, showing a clear ability to distinguish blue and yellow <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kasparson et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Pongrácz et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This visual system is similar to humans who have deuteranopia (red-green color blindness) (Siniscalchi et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This visual system is similar to humans who have deuteranopia (red-green color blindness) <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Siniscalchi et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Color appearance, however, depends on a number of physical and perceptual properties including hue and brightness (Fairchild, 2013).
text.formatted: Color appearance, however, depends on a number of physical and perceptual properties including hue and brightness <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fairchild, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Hue is characterized by the dominant wavelength of light perceived and how much it appears to be similar to one of the colors red, yellow, green, and blue.
Brightness is the perception of how much light a source reflects (in contrast to the purely physical properties of luminance and reflectance).
Discrimination work has informed our understanding of how dogs prioritize color/hue and brightness cues.
Dogs appear to rely on color/hue cues over brightness cues when discriminating between physical stimuli (Kasparson et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Dogs appear to rely on color/hue cues over brightness cues when discriminating between physical stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kasparson et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: However, brightness becomes more relevant when stimuli are presented on computer screens.
At certain brightness levels, dogs struggle to differentiate colored stimuli (Byosiere et al., 2019).
text.formatted: At certain brightness levels, dogs struggle to differentiate colored stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Byosiere et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We do not yet fully understand how color/hue and brightness cues combine to influence dog perception and behavior.

In addition to studying which properties of color underlie dogs' ability to discriminate stimuli, researchers also investigate whether dogs have preferences for specific colors. Roy et al. (2025) investigated whether Indian free-ranging dogs preferred to eat out of blue, yellow, or grey bowls.
text.formatted: In addition to studying which properties of color underlie dogs' ability to discriminate stimuli, researchers also investigate whether dogs have preferences for specific colors. <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> investigated whether Indian free-ranging dogs preferred to eat out of blue, yellow, or grey bowls.

text.text: They offered each dog all three colored bowls at the same time and recorded the bowl that the dogs investigated first as their choice.
In one condition, each bowl contained a treat, whereas in another condition, no bowls contained treats.
Each dog only completed a single trial so that the food reward (if present) would not influence future choices.
Across 134 dogs, Roy et al. observed a strong preference for the yellow bowl independent of the presence of food.
The authors proposed possible adaptive explanations for the preference.

The species-confidence hypothesis suggests that many free-ranging dogs have yellow/orange/brown coats, but none have blue coats, so yellow is preferred because it is cue for conspecifics (e.g., in a mating context).
The ecological valence theory proposes that preference is tied to the ecological value of objects in the environment.
The authors suggest that in the dog's visual system, the red/pink color of raw meat and blood may appear yellowish, which could drive the preferences.
Relatedly, an learning-based account may underlie the preference because the yellow spice tumeric is frequently used in Indian cooking.
Dogs may therefore associate the color yellow with food obtained in human trash.
Regardless of whether there is an adaptive or associate account, across multiple studies, Roy et al. show a preference for yellow-colored bowls.
It is not clear, however, whether this preference for yellow is shared across other types of dogs in different locations or whether it is based on the experience of being a free-ranging dog in India.
Moreover, it is unclear whether the preference is for the hue of yellow or whether it could be driven by some other property such as brightness.

Visual inspection of Figure 1 in Roy et al. gives the subjective impression that the brightness for the yellow option is higher than the other two colors, and Roy et al. suggest that the yellow may "pop out" more than the other colors.
text.formatted: Visual inspection of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> in <ref type="bibr">Roy et al.</ref> gives the subjective impression that the brightness for the yellow option is higher than the other two colors, and Roy et al. suggest that the yellow may "pop out" more than the other colors.

text.text: This subjective experience inspired us to investigate whether the choice of yellow could be driven by brightness rather than hue.

In this study, we replicated the work by Roy et al. (2025) in a new population of dogs in a set of three preregistered studies that investigated whether pet dogs in the United States demonstrate a color preference.
text.formatted: In this study, we replicated the work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> in a new population of dogs in a set of three preregistered studies that investigated whether pet dogs in the United States demonstrate a color preference.

text.text: In Experiment 1, we replicated Roy et al.'s methods to determine whether dogs choose a yellow bowl over a blue or grey bowl when presented with the three colors.

After observing preliminary evidence for possibly different choices between younger and older dogs in an exploratory analysis of Experiment 1, we hypothesized that younger dogs would choose a yellow bowl over a blue or grey bowl.
In Experiment 2, we replicated Experiment 1 but preregistered a restriction for recruiting younger dogs.
Following Roy et al., we also hypothesized and preregistered that the presence of food, sex, and bowl position will not affect the color preference.

Lastly, we extended Roy et al. by investigating the potential role of brightness in dog color preference by presenting dogs with three grey bowls of varying brightness levels: light, medium, and dark grey.
We hypothesized and preregistered that younger dogs would choose the brightest bowl over either of the two darker bowls.
Combined, these studies assess the generalizability of the Roy et al. findings to a new population and investigate whether brightness instead of color/hue may drive the effects.
This study was conducted at multiple outdoor locations: four dog parks, one city park, and one dog bar with a fenced in lawn in Lincoln, Nebraska, USA.
At each testing location, experimenters identified a grassy area with minimal potential distractors and no direct shade from trees, buildings, etc.
We used the same experimental setup across all testing locations.
The study ran during daylight hours (09:00-20:00 h) from May 2025 to June 2025.
We collected data from 95 dogs with 48.4% being female, 90.4% being neutered/spayed, and a mean (±standard deviation) age of 3.9±3.1 years.
We excluded 19 dogs due to failing to complete the warm-up trial (n=12) or failing to choose in the experimental trial (n=7), resulting in 76 dogs with complete data.
To follow our preregistration and match the sample size in the food condition of Roy et al. (2025), we only analyzed data from the first 75 dogs that we tested.
text.formatted: To follow our preregistration and match the sample size in the food condition of <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref>, we only analyzed data from the first 75 dogs that we tested.

text.text: As a sensitivity analysis, we re-ran analyses with all 76 dogs and found the same results.
We used three terracotta bowls (diameter 12.5 cm, height 5.7 cm) painted with Apple Barrel Gloss non-toxic acrylic paint.
We painted each bowl either Golden Yellow (21395E), Real Blue (20660E), or Dark Gray (20366E).
We used a Shimadzu UV-2501 spectrophotometer with an integrating sphere for specular reflectance (Model ISR-2200) to measure color absorbance and percent reflectivity (Figure 1).
text.formatted: We used a Shimadzu UV-2501 spectrophotometer with an integrating sphere for specular reflectance (Model ISR-2200) to measure color absorbance and percent reflectivity (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Absorbance offers the amount of light at each wavelength absorbed by the bowls of different colors, whereas reflectivity measures the percent of each wavelength reflected from the bowls.
Color absorbance and percent reflectivity measure physical properties of the paint not the perception of color or brightness for dogs.
We used BaSO4 as a background for both measurements.
Yellow showed peak absorbance at 450 nm and peak reflectivity at 612 nm.
Blue showed peak absorbance at 569 nm and peak reflectivity at 452 nm.
Grey (shown as medium grey in Figure 1) showed peak absorbance at 401 nm and peak reflectivity at 537 nm.
text.formatted: Grey (shown as medium grey in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) showed peak absorbance at 401 nm and peak reflectivity at 537 nm.

text.text: Absorbance and Reflectivity of Bowl Colors Note. (a) Absorbance and (b) percent reflectivity as a function of wavelength in nm for yellow, blue, light grey, medium grey, and dark grey paint.
We attached the bowls with Velcro to a 70 × 17 cm wooden board spaced about 15 cm apart with a circle drawn 2 cm out from each bowl (Figure 2a).
text.formatted: We attached the bowls with Velcro to a 70 × 17 cm wooden board spaced about 15 cm apart with a circle drawn 2 cm out from each bowl (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2a</ref>).

text.text: The bowls were located closer to one of the long edges of the board than the other to allow room for the treat in the warm-up trials.
We refer to the long edge of the board that is further from the bowl locations as the "dog side" of the board and the edge closer to the bowl locations as the "experimenter side".
An opaque black plastic occluder (121 × 46 cm) blocked the dog's line of sight during experimental setup.
We used Pet Botanics Soft & Chewy Beef Flavor Training Rewards treats.
text.formatted: We used Pet Botanics Soft & Chewy Beef Flavor Training Rewards treats.

text.text: We recorded sessions with a GoPro HERO9 Black camera on a Sunpak 7001 D tripod placed 2 m behind the "experimenter side" of the board.
Experimental Set-Up.
Two experimenters conducted each experimental trial.
Experimenters wore neutral-colored shirts (white/black, no colors) for all experimental sessions.
Experimenter 1 presented the dog with the experimental stimuli, and Experimenter 2 recorded the data.
All experimenters rotated between the roles of Experimenter 1 and 2 throughout the study.
All experimenters had read Roy et al. (2025) and therefore were not blind to the hypotheses.
text.formatted: All experimenters had read <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> and therefore were not blind to the hypotheses.

text.text: To begin the set-up, experimenters placed the wooden board in a grassy area at the testing location.
Experimenters placed two leashes on the ground 2 m away from and parallel to the board with one on either side (Figure 2b).
text.formatted: Experimenters placed two leashes on the ground 2 m away from and parallel to the board with one on either side (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2b</ref>).

text.text: These leashes acted as a starting line for the dog and a line for Experimenter 1 to wait behind during the dog's choice.
A third 2.75 m leash connected the dog to the base of a camping chair that the owner sat in.
Before each trial, experimenters placed the three bowls in the appropriate randomized color Experimental Set-Up Note. (a) Grey, yellow, and blue bowls on wooden tray used in Experiments 1 and 2.

Circles on board represent 2 cm choice area. (b) Schematic showing owner holding dog, red leashes as starting lines, experimenter behind the occluder, tray of bowls, and camera. (c) Light, medium, and dark grey bowls on wooden tray used in Experiment 3.
order on the board (counterbalanced across subjects).
An occluder blocked visibility of the board from the "dog side".
The owner sat in the camping chair with their dog in front of them facing toward the board (Figure 2b).
text.formatted: The owner sat in the camping chair with their dog in front of them facing toward the board (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2b</ref>).

text.text: Experimenter 2 clipped the leash attached to the base of the chair to the dog's collar/harness.
The owner held the dog (by leash or collar) at the start line.
With the occluder in place, Experimenter 1 crouched on the "experimenter side" of the board and placed a treat in front of each bowl location.
Experimenter 1 called the dog's name to get their attention before lifting the occluder and placing it between the treats and the bowls on the board.
This made the treats visible to the dog while still occluding the bowls.
Experimenter 1 kept their gaze on the ground and waited for three seconds.
After the pause, Experimenter 1 said "now" and the owner released the dog to approach the treats.
If the dog approached the board right away to eat the treats, the warm-up ended.
If the dog was hesitant to approach, the experimenters tapped on the board to draw the dog's attention or hand-fed one of the treats to the dog (n=6).
The warm-ups were successfully completed if the dog eventually ate all three treats and at least one of them was on the board (not hand-fed).
Only dogs that successfully completed the warm-up continued to participate in the experimental trial.
Experimental Trial.
After successful completion of the warm-up, the owner recalled the dog back to the starting line.
Experimenter 1 crouched on the "experimenter side" of the board and put one treat in each of the three bowls on the board behind the occluder.
To begin the trial, Experimenter 1 called the dog's name to get their attention.
Then Experimenter 1 lifted the occluder, diverted their gaze to the ground, and walked backward in a crouch with the occluder until they were between the leash and the tripod.
Once behind the leash and still looking at the ground, Experimenter 1 waited three seconds before saying "now", signaling the owner to release their dog to approach the bowls.
Experimenter 2 recorded the order that the dog chose the bowls in (e.g. yellow, then blue, then grey).

text.text: Because this study was conducted throughout the day and over a seven month period, differences in lighting levels over the course of the day and across seasons could vary resulting in different illumination of the colors.
To assess this possibility, we conducted a model selection procedure for a set of logistic regressions.
First, we created a new outcome variable that coded any trials in which the dog chose yellow first as a 1 and either blue or grey first as a 0.
Therefore, our outcome variable was the probability of choosing yellow first over the other colors.
We then extracted the hour of the day from our data as well as the date.
We recoded the dates by subtracting the first date from each subsequent date, result in the number of days from our first trial.
We then conducted a series of logistic regressions with the probability of yellow as our outcome variable.
We included an intercept only model, hour only, date only, and hour, date, and the hour by date interaction model.
In addition, we included those same models with second-degree polynomial versions of hour and date, resulting in a total of nine models.
We used the test_performance() function from the performance package (Lüdecke et al., 2021) to calculate the Bayes factor comparing each model to the intercept only model.

Therefore, we found no evidence that time of day or date influenced the probability of choosing yellow.

text.text: The primary aim of this study was to replicate Roy et al. (2025) to assess whether pet dogs in the United States also preferred yellow over blue or grey.
text.formatted: The primary aim of this study was to replicate <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> to assess whether pet dogs in the United States also preferred yellow over blue or grey.

text.text: We tested this with three preregistered experiments.
In Experiment 1, we did not find a strong preference for yellow.
However, our sample included dogs with no age restrictions, likely differing from Roy et al.'s sample of free-ranging dogs.
An exploratory analysis that restricted to dogs younger than seven years old suggested that they might prefer yellow, but the sample size was too small to strongly test this.
In Experiment 2, we restricted the sample to dogs under seven years old and replicated Roy et al.'s finding that dogs chose yellow bowls first most often.
This preference was not affected by the presence of food, sex, or the spatial position of the bowls.
Experiment 3 tested preferences between light, medium, and dark grey investigating whether the preference for yellow was actually driven by brightness rather than hue.
We did not find a preference for light grey and, if anything, there was a preference for dark grey, not supporting brightness as a driving factor for the observed preference for yellow.
Taken together, our experiments suggest that young dogs have a preference for yellow over blue bowls, replicating Roy et al. (2025).
text.formatted: Taken together, our experiments suggest that young dogs have a preference for yellow over blue bowls, replicating <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern is not explained by a lower-level preference for brighter stimuli.

Though the overall findings align with Roy et al., our effects were not as strong or universal as observed previously. Roy et al. found that more than half of their dogs preferred yellow, and blue and grey were equally preferred.
text.formatted: Though the overall findings align with Roy et al., our effects were not as strong or universal as observed previously. <ref type="bibr">Roy et al.</ref> found that more than half of their dogs preferred yellow, and blue and grey were equally preferred.

text.text: We found a preference for yellow over blue, but we found an intermediate preference for grey.
Nonetheless, young companion dogs in Nebraska and free-ranging dogs in India do appear to show an affinity for yellow bowls.
This begs the question: Why do dogs prefer yellow?
Roy et al. proposed two adaptive and one associative explanation for a preference for yellow.
Here, we speculate on other possible explanations for this preference that warrant further investigation.
Research on human and macaque visual systems have revealed notable properties of the color yellow.
In humans, yellow is processed more quickly and accurately than the color blue (Wool et al., 2015).

text.text: Macaques, too, display a faster and greater amplitude of visual cortex activity in response to yellow compared to blue (Wool et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Macaques, too, display a faster and greater amplitude of visual cortex activity in response to yellow compared to blue <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Wool et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: So, while we interpret our findings as preference, speed of processing may also shape which color is approached first.
However, we do not know whether dogs have the same color processing as humans and macaques.
Humans may also interpret the colors blue and yellow differently.
When viewing objects, humans tend to interpret a bluish tint as a property of the lighting and a yellowish tint as a property of the object itself (Webster, 2020).
text.formatted: When viewing objects, humans tend to interpret a bluish tint as a property of the lighting and a yellowish tint as a property of the object itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Webster, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: How our brains react to the colors blue and yellow is likely rooted in our real-world experiences, as shadows from natural light take on a blue tint and objects themselves have warmer tints (Webster, 2020).
text.formatted: How our brains react to the colors blue and yellow is likely rooted in our real-world experiences, as shadows from natural light take on a blue tint and objects themselves have warmer tints <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Webster, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, yellow may be chosen in this context because it is interpreted as a property of objects.

Lastly, humans show strong associations between colors and odors, emotions, and concepts (Österbauer et al., 2005; Mohammad, 2011; Tham et al., 2020), though these can vary across cultures (Barchard et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Lastly, humans show strong associations between colors and odors, emotions, and concepts <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Österbauer et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Mohammad, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Tham et al., 2020)</ref>, though these can vary across cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barchard et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Just as we associate the color yellow with familiar odor stimuli (e.g., lemon or banana), dogs could have similar associations with relevant stimuli in their environment.

The fact that we also found a preference for yellow in pet dogs in the United States suggests that either (1) Roy et al.'s (2025) findings were not due to something unique about the free-ranging dog experience in India but to something more general about dog preferences or (2) the same associations were made across these two populations.
text.formatted: The fact that we also found a preference for yellow in pet dogs in the United States suggests that either (1) <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al.'s (2025)</ref> findings were not due to something unique about the free-ranging dog experience in India but to something more general about dog preferences or (2) the same associations were made across these two populations.

text.text: A shared association seems less likely given the different environments experienced by these two populations.
This leaves open the reason why dogs prefer yellow.
Though the color yellow differs in hue from blue, it also typically differs in brightness.
The yellow bowl in Figure 1 of Roy et al. (2025) appears to be brighter than their blue bowl.
text.formatted: The yellow bowl in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> of <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> appears to be brighter than their blue bowl.

text.text: The blue used in our study is brighter than Roy et al.'s, but it is still darker than our yellow (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The blue used in our study is brighter than Roy et al.'s, but it is still darker than our yellow (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: We investigated whether brightness could account for our finding a preference for yellow over blue by offering dogs three different shades of grey that vary in brightness.
However, we did not find a difference between the shades, though a more highly powered design might have suggested a preference for the darkest shade of grey.
Therefore, we did not find evidence for brightness accounting for the preference for yellow over blue.
There are a few possibilities for why we did not find evidence for brightness driving the preference.
First, our test of brightness moved from chromatic (yellow, blue) to achromatic (grey) hues.
In an effort to completely control brightness, we removed color, which may result in different preferences.
That is, the preference for yellow could have resulted from an interaction between hue and brightness, and removing chromatic hue might change the dynamics.
A follow-up study offering choices between different shades of yellow could help address this.
Also, offering choices between yellow, blue, and grey with equal brightness would be useful, though accomplishing this with paint can be tricky when trying to create exact brightness values.
Computer-generated colors would simplify maintaining constant brightness, though preference may be more difficult to assess with computer stimuli.
Moreover, brightness is more of a subjective than objective, physical measure-it is the perception of how much light is reflected.
Thus, measures of brightness based on human vision may not carry over to canine vision.
A second possibility for the lack of a brightness effect could be because dogs react more strongly to hue than brightness.
Two discrimination studies in dogs varied both hue and brightness found that hue drove their behavior more than brightness (Kasparson et al., 2013; Byosiere et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Two discrimination studies in dogs varied both hue and brightness found that hue drove their behavior more than brightness <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kasparson et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Byosiere et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This would make sense if hue has a stronger functional benefit than brightness, but further work is needed to support this.
In Experiment 1, we did not restrict ages.
But upon faceting the data based on age (Figure 3b), we noticed that younger dogs seemed to show a yellow preference but older dogs did not.
text.formatted: But upon faceting the data based on age (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3b</ref>), we noticed that younger dogs seemed to show a yellow preference but older dogs did not.

text.text: We restricted the age of subjects to under seven years old in Experiment 2 and found a preference for yellow.

Though we do not have good estimates for ages in the dogs in the Roy et al. (2025) study or for the Indian free-ranging dogs more generally, a study of free-ranging dogs in Baltimore, Maryland, USA showed a maximum age of seven years (Beck, 1973).

(2025)</ref> study or for the Indian free-ranging dogs more generally, a study of free-ranging dogs in Baltimore, Maryland, USA showed a maximum age of seven years <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beck, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, by restricting our analyses to dogs under seven years old, we are likely more closely matching the age distribution found in Roy et al. In addition to matching the original study demographics, age could be an important influence on the color preference itself.
text.formatted: Thus, by restricting our analyses to dogs under seven years old, we are likely more closely matching the age distribution found in <ref type="bibr">Roy et al.</ref> In addition to matching the original study demographics, age could be an important influence on the color preference itself.

text.text: Little work has investigated age effects on color perception or preferences in dogs.

However, studies on other aspects of visual anatomy and cognition indicate a decline with age (Head et al., 1998; Milfont & Gouveia, 2006; Studzinski et al., 2006; Snigdha et al., 2012; Szabó et al., 2018; Barber et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, studies on other aspects of visual anatomy and cognition indicate a decline with age <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Head et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Milfont & Gouveia, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Studzinski et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Snigdha et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Szabó et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Barber et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Humans show impairments in color perception as they age (Faubert & Bellefeuille, 2002; Han et al., 2016) and also prefer a saturated yellow over dark blue when young but find them equally preferable when older (Zhang et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Humans show impairments in color perception as they age <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Faubert & Bellefeuille, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Han et al., 2016)</ref> and also prefer a saturated yellow over dark blue when young but find them equally preferable when older <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Zhang et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the age effects we observe in dogs might reflect differences in color preferences over their lifespan.
However, this analysis is exploratory and has a small sample size, so future work is need to verify potential age effects.
Color preferences in dogs are not just academic or aesthetic-they can be useful in designing dog toys, environments, and research sessions.
Knowing what colors dogs can discriminate or prefer could be useful for dog toy manufacturers to help guide the design of toys that maximally engage dogs' attention.
Currently, dog toys are likely designed with humans in mind, since we are the ones who buy the toys (Coren, 2025).
text.formatted: Currently, dog toys are likely designed with humans in mind, since we are the ones who buy the toys <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Coren, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Tests of toy color preferences could be useful to the dog toy industry to determine whether dogs' preferences differ from their owners'.
Future research should investigate whether color preferences could also be useful in designing dog living areas.
Shelters, for example, usually want to create a calming environment for dogs that face the stressful experience of being in a shelter.
If dogs prefer some colors over others, it is possible that those colors may influence their physiology, which can affect their well-being.
Shelters could explore whether painting their walls colors that dogs perceive as calming influences their physiology and/or behavior.
Finally, for canine behavioral scientists, understanding color preferences is critical because we frequently choose colors for stimuli that we present to subjects.

If researchers present stimuli of different colors, preference for a particular color could bias results toward that stimulus and skew the results based on what should be an arbitrary logistical choice rather than research-relevant properties under investigation.
This fact is what inspired us to replicate Roy et al. (2025), and given their and our findings, color is an important variable that must be considered carefully and counterbalanced across stimuli.
text.formatted: This fact is what inspired us to replicate <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref>, and given their and our findings, color is an important variable that must be considered carefully and counterbalanced across stimuli.

text.text: There are a number of considerations to keep in mind with our findings.
First, we tried to directly replicate the methods of Roy et al. (2025), which included simultaneously presenting bowls of three colors.
text.formatted: First, we tried to directly replicate the methods of <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref>, which included simultaneously presenting bowls of three colors.

text.text: Like Roy et al., we only used three colors, though these are the three primary colors that dogs can see (Pongrácz et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Like Roy et al., we only used three colors, though these are the three primary colors that dogs can see <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Pongrácz et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Testing additional colors would be useful, even for hues that may be perceived similarly (e.g., red and green).
Other components such as brightness and saturation may influence preferences.
Including more hues using multiple pairwise comparisons of hues would provide a more sophisticated measure of color preference.
Having multiple trials within subjects would provide important test-retest reliability measures to assess the stability of preference.
Another consideration for our work deals with odor.
Dogs have outstanding olfactory abilities (Johnen et al., 2013; Lazarowski, 2023), and different paint colors are created with pigments generated from different chemical compounds.
text.formatted: Dogs have outstanding olfactory abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Johnen et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lazarowski, 2023)</ref>, and different paint colors are created with pigments generated from different chemical compounds.

text.text: Though undetectable to us, it is possible that the pigments produce different odors, and dogs could have actually been demonstrating a preference for the odor of the yellow paint.
This could explain why the dogs in Roy et al. (2025) showed a stronger preference for yellow than our dogs.
text.formatted: This could explain why the dogs in <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> showed a stronger preference for yellow than our dogs.

text.text: If our paints were composed of different chemicals, their yellow paint might have smelled "better" than our yellow paint.
Roy et al. conducted an odor control preference test where they covered yellow and blue bowls with magenta sleeves.
They did not find a preference for the underlying yellow bowls, suggesting odor did not drive their findings.
In another test, they put food in a grey bowl but not a yellow bowl, and the dogs still preferred the yellow bowl, choosing color over food odor.
Moreover, studies show that dogs tend to use visual over olfactory cues in vision-based tasks (Szetei et al., 2003; Bräuer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, studies show that dogs tend to use visual over olfactory cues in vision-based tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Szetei et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bräuer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, to fully control for odor cues, researchers should either use non-pigment-based paints or use computer-generated colors to test dog color preferences.
Our data clearly showed individual differences in the color chosen first.
In examining the combined data (Figure 5a), there is an almost two-fold stronger preference for yellow over blue (91 vs. 49 dogs; 1.86 ratio).
text.formatted: In examining the combined data (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5a</ref>), there is an almost two-fold stronger preference for yellow over blue (91 vs. 49 dogs; 1.86 ratio).

text.text: However, there is not a difference between preference for yellow and grey (74 dogs).
The preference for yellow in our data is slightly smaller than that in Roy et al. (2025) (72 yellow vs. 30 blue; 2.40 ratio).
text.formatted: The preference for yellow in our data is slightly smaller than that in <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> (72 yellow vs. 30 blue; 2.40 ratio).

text.text: Onetrial measures of preferences are noisy.
Our data could reflect individual differences in color preferences or individual differences in attending to experimental stimuli.
Thus, the preference could be stronger if dogs paid more attention to the color of the bowls before approaching.
Another factor that could account for preferences is the dogs' experiences with different colors.
If dogs have food bowls, toys, walls, or food itself that is yellow, dogs could associate the color yellow with food.
Given the wide range of possible environmental variables where color could play a role, we did not assess our subjects' experiences with different colors.
Future studies to try to assess dogs' exposure to and experience with different colors to investigate whether these influence color preferences.
The aim of this study was to replicate Roy et al. (2025), which focused on the context of food.
text.formatted: The aim of this study was to replicate <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref>, which focused on the context of food.

text.text: Because colors may have associations with food, these results may not generalize beyond food contexts.
That is, dogs may not have a preference for yellow generally but may when food is involved.

To test general color preferences, researchers should conduct color preference tests with other objects, such as dog toys to determine whether food preferences generalize to toys, wall paints, or other objects.
A final consideration is our study population.
Our study sampled dogs at dog parks, a city park, a dog bar, a dog show, and a dog daycare.
A key advantage of the recruitment method is that is mimics the design of Roy et al. (2025) by having dogs participate in an outdoor environment.
text.formatted: A key advantage of the recruitment method is that is mimics the design of <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> by having dogs participate in an outdoor environment.

text.text: This contrasts with many studies of dog behavior that test in laboratory environments, which are different from outdoor tests.
Typical lab-based experiments sample a fairly select subgroup of dog owners: those who have the interest in and means to bring their dogs to a dog lab (Espinosa et al., in press).
text.formatted: Typical lab-based experiments sample a fairly select subgroup of dog owners: those who have the interest in and means to bring their dogs to a dog lab <ref type="bibr">(Espinosa et al., in press)</ref>.

text.text: The sample for this study is slightly different but also potentially unique.
In our outdoor testing locations, dog are likely more familiar and comfortable with their testing environment than in laboratory environments.
However, the population of dogs in our sample likely differs from that in typical laboratory studies and the dog population in general.
Testing at dog parks could bias our sample toward a specific subset of dogs, in particular dogs whose owners want to go to dog parks.
This could result in a sample skewed toward more social or more active dogs.

Therefore, though our replication of Roy et al. generalizes their findings to pet dogs in the United States, we must keep the test population in mind and highlight that these findings may not generalize across all pet dogs in the United States.
Also, we used treats to draw attention to the apparatus.
So, our sample favored food-motivated dogs because those with low food interest likely did not complete the warm-up trial and advance to the experimental trial, thus further restricting our sample.
This was especially evident when we tested outside a dog show.
Many of the show dogs were used to very high-quality treats to keep their motivation during shows.
Several of them were not interested in our rather mid-quality treats, and therefore those dogs were not included in our data.

Despite the possibility of our data coming from a narrow subpopulation of dogs, our overall findings replicated those of Roy et al. (2025), suggesting that a color preference for yellow generalizes from free-ranging dogs in India to pet dogs in the United States.

(2025)</ref>, suggesting that a color preference for yellow generalizes from free-ranging dogs in India to pet dogs in the United States.

text.text: Nevertheless, testing dogs in other geographical locations and social situations would further investigate the generalizability of color preferences.
Our study replicated the Roy et al. (2025) finding that dogs approached a yellow bowl first, suggesting that this color preference extends to the younger pet dogs sampled here.
text.formatted: Our study replicated the <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Roy et al. (2025)</ref> finding that dogs approached a yellow bowl first, suggesting that this color preference extends to the younger pet dogs sampled here.

text.text: Though this is only two populations, it hints to the possibility that a preference for yellow in this food context may be general to domestic dogs.
Future work across other populations is needed to confirm the extent of this preference.
We did not find evidence for color preference depending on presence of food, sex, dog breed type, weather/lighting conditions, or spatial position.
We did not find that stimulus brightness could account for our findings; however, we removed color from our brightness test, and brightness may interact with color to influence preference.
We only found the preference for yellow bowls in younger dogs, raising the possibility of age-related differences in color preference, which require direct testing.

This preference for yellow may be due to low-level visual processing in the brain, though most of the work on these features occurs in species with three color photoreceptors, so more work is needed in dogs and other species with two color photoreceptors.
Understanding color preferences in dogs is important for both their welfare and the integrity of research studying them.
Knowing which colors they prefer can inform how to design both toys and environments meant to calm dogs (e.g., shelters).
And researchers should consider color preferences when designing studies, especially when having dogs choose between multiple stimuli of different colors.
